description: system.usage.* value semantics that no JSON Schema can assert (PROTOCOL_SPEC 6.7.1). The two schemas sys-usage-summary/sys-usage-module lock the SHAPE; a full-history call_count and an off-by-one p99_latency_ms are both well-typed numbers in the right field, so they need fixed inputs and expected outputs instead. Cases 1-3 pin the p99 disagreement (apcore-python returned sorted[rank] where apcore-typescript and apcore-rust returned sorted[rank-1]); cases 4-6 pin that `period` filters rather than being echoed (apcore-rust echoed it and computed over the full retained history); cases 7-9 pin the period grammar at the input-validation boundary; case 10 pins the hour-key format and the 24-entry invariant; case 11 pins the unattributed caller_id.

driver_contract.path: MUST drive the real UsageCollector and the real system.usage.* modules through Executor.call() — not the collector's internal accessors directly. Every divergence this fixture pins lives in the sys-module layer's choice of accessor (apcore-rust called get_all_summaries() where a period-aware variant existed), so a driver that calls get_summary_for_period() itself asserts the layer that was never wrong.
driver_contract.clock: `records[].at_offset` is relative to the moment the driver runs: '-2h' means two hours ago. Every SDK can inject that -- apcore-python and apcore-typescript take an optional `timestamp` on `record()`, apcore-rust has `record_at()`. A driver that ignores the offset and records everything at `now` cannot distinguish a period-filtering implementation from one that summarises all of history, which is the divergence this fixture exists to pin.
driver_contract.p99_is_not_a_schema_assertion: Cases 1-3 supply the exact latency list and the exact expected value. Asserting `type(p99) == number` passes against every implementation including the wrong ones. Assert the VALUE.
driver_contract.period_rejection_is_a_wire_code: Cases 7-9 expect SCHEMA_VALIDATION_ERROR from input validation, NOT a language-native ValueError/Error from a private parser. A driver asserting only 'it raised' would be green against all three of today's mutually incompatible behaviours.
driver_contract.module_id_is_opaque: `module_id` is an opaque identifier the driver registers as a no-op module. The detail module looks it up in the registry before reporting, so it must exist.
driver_contract.unattributed_caller: `caller_id: null` MUST be produced through the SDK's own usage-recording path for a call whose Context carries no caller identity -- i.e. UsageMiddleware, or whatever records usage in that SDK. It MUST NOT be produced by handing a null/None straight to UsageCollector.record(): apcore-python and apcore-typescript type that parameter as a string and substitute 'unknown' in the middleware, while apcore-rust takes Option<&str> and substitutes in the breakdown. Driving the collector directly therefore tests three different APIs and fails on two of them for a reason that has nothing to do with the contract.

test_cases.note: N=1, rank=ceil(0.99)=1, index=0. The clamp is what keeps this in range.
0, not null — the field is required and typed number in the canonical schema.
The 2026-03-06 record is outside the 24h window. An implementation covering the full history answers 2.
callers[] and p99 must be period-filtered too, not only the top-level counts. The out-of-window record would move p99 to 500 and add a second caller.
The control case for the two above. Without it, an implementation that returns nothing at all passes the filtering cases for the wrong reason.
Leading [1-9] is normative. apcore-python accepted this and returned an all-zero report that reads as 'no traffic'.
apcore-python accepted this (int('-5')); apcore-typescript's anchored regex rejected it.

Keys are YYYY-MM-DDTHH -- apcore-rust emitted 2026-03-08T10:00:00Z, and this repository's own docs showed that spelling. Exactly 24 entries covering now-23h..now, ascending, gaps zero-filled. The concrete keys depend on when the suite runs, so the driver asserts the FORMAT and the invariants, not literal hour strings.

PROTOCOL_SPEC 6.7.1.4. `caller_id: null` means a CALL WITH NO CALLER IDENTITY, not a literal null passed to the collector: the SDKs place the substitution at different layers -- apcore-python and apcore-typescript in UsageMiddleware, apcore-rust in the caller breakdown, since its record() takes Option<&str>. The observable contract is the same and that is what is asserted; see driver_contract.unattributed_caller. Only caller_ids is asserted: the recording path measures real elapsed time, so a latency this fixture chose would be unassertable through it.
